- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

/**
 * Port of `whoosh.analysis.filters.STOP_WORDS`.
 *
 * Whoosh's default English stop list is deliberately TINY (34 entries) compared
 * with, say, NLTK's ~179-word list: Whoosh started life as a documentation /
 * help-file indexer, which is also why the decidedly non-prose entry 'tbd' is in
 * here. Do not "improve" this list - it is used symmetrically at index time and
 * at query time, so any change silently alters which documents match without
 * ever raising an error.
 *
 * Words that people often expect but which are NOT in Whoosh's list (do not add
 * them): was, were, been, but, they, he, she, his, her, all, would, there, what,
 * which, who, how, do, no, so, than, then, these.
 *
 * The list is applied AFTER LowercaseFilter in StandardAnalyzer, so every entry
 * is lowercase. Any single-character entry would be redundant anyway because
 * StopFilter's default minsize=2 already drops 1-character tokens.
 */

/** @type {ReadonlySet<string>} Whoosh's default English stop list (34 words). */
export const STOP_WORDS = new Set([
  'a',
  'an',
  'and',
  'are',
  'as',
  'at',
  'be',
  'by',
  'can',
  'for',
  'from',
  'have',
  'if',
  'in',
  'is',
  'it',
  'may',
  'not',
  'of',
  'on',
  'or',
  'tbd',
  'that',
  'the',
  'this',
  'to',
  'us',
  'we',
  'when',
  'will',
  'with',
  'yet',
  'you',
  'your',
]);

// Whoosh exposes this as a frozenset. JS cannot freeze a Set's contents, but we
// at least freeze the object so nobody bolts extra properties onto it. Treat the
// set itself as immutable: pass a copy to StopFilter if you need a variant list.
Object.freeze(STOP_WORDS);

export default STOP_WORDS;

content.text: All five modules are written, syntax-checked, and differentially validated against CPython 3.12's `re` (25/25 inputs byte-identical on both raw tokens and full StandardAnalyzer output).

exports_provided: token.mjs: Token (class, with copy() and toString()); plus a `default` alias for Token
stopwords.mjs: STOP_WORDS (frozen Set, exactly the 34 contract words); plus a `default` alias
tokenizers.mjs: DEFAULT_WORD_PATTERN (RegExp /[\p{L}\p{N}_]+(?:\.?[\p{L}\p{N}_]+)*/gu), Tokenizer, RegexTokenizer, IDTokenizer, SpaceSeparatedTokenizer
analyzers.mjs: Analyzer, CompositeAnalyzer, StandardAnalyzer(), SimpleAnalyzer(), IDAnalyzer(), KeywordAnalyzer()
deviations: Token identity: tokenizers allocate a FRESH Token per token instead of Whoosh's single recycled instance (explicitly permitted by the brief; documented at the top of token.mjs). Filters still mutate-and-re-yield the token they receive, which is safe precisely because each is distinct. Consequence: [...analyzer.analyze(v)] is safe here but would collapse in real Whoosh.

IDTokenizer yields ZERO tokens for the empty string. Whoosh's source yields one token unconditionally (producing an empty-string term); the research phase flagged that nuance as unverified and my brief says empty input should yield no tokens. Irrelevant to test11 (ID is imported but never used).

IDTokenizer sets pos = start_pos (0-based). I recall Whoosh's source using start_pos + 1 there, but only at medium confidence, so I chose the self-consistent numbering rather than reproduce a possibly-misremembered off-by-one. Only observable for an ID field indexed with positions.

SpaceSeparatedTokenizer extends RegexTokenizer (which extends Tokenizer) rather than extending Tokenizer directly — this mirrors Whoosh, where it IS RegexTokenizer(r"[^ \t\r\n]+"). `instanceof Tokenizer` still holds.

IDAnalyzer() and KeywordAnalyzer() always return a CompositeAnalyzer wrapper. Whoosh returns the bare tokenizer when there are no filters; the contract requires every analyzer instance to have .analyze(), so the wrapper guarantees it. As extra insurance, Tokenizer also exposes analyze() (delegating to tokenize()), so a bare tokenizer handed to fieldtypes as an analyzer still works — this mirrors Whoosh's Composable duck-typing.

Contract's tokenize() option list is implemented as a superset: I also honor Whoosh's `tokenize: false` kwarg (emit the whole value as one token, original set unconditionally). Unknown option keys are ignored.

KeywordAnalyzer({commas: true}) folds Whoosh's StripFilter into the pattern (/[^,\s](?:[^,]*[^,\s])?/), so a whitespace-only comma field yields no token where Whoosh would yield an empty-string token.

StopFilter does not accept Whoosh's `lang` parameter (not in the contract); it takes only {stoplist, minsize, maxsize, renumber}. It accepts any iterable stoplist (Set/Array), treats stoplist null/empty as 'no stop list, minsize still applies', and treats maxsize null/0 as unbounded (Whoosh's falsy-maxsize convention).
minsize/maxsize compare CODE POINT length, not .length, to match Python len(). An astral-plane single character is therefore dropped (Python parity) rather than kept.

Extra `export default` on token.mjs and stopwords.mjs (additive only — `export *` in the barrel ignores defaults). Purely so a sibling agent writing `import Token from './token.mjs'` gets the class rather than undefined.

Defensive behavior beyond Whoosh (which asserts isinstance(value, str)): non-string values are coerced with String() (null/undefined -> ''), an uncompilable user expression falls back to DEFAULT_WORD_SOURCE instead of throwing, the `u` flag is added only when the pattern is `u`-compatible, sticky `y` is stripped, zero-width matches advance by one full code point (no infinite loop), and malformed/null tokens inside a filter are tolerated. Nothing in this module group can throw.
input.notes:
VERIFICATION (not just syntax): I ran a differential against CPython 3.12.3's `re` using the real Whoosh pattern r"\w+(\.?\w+)*" plus a hand-rolled lowercase+stoplist+minsize chain over 25 discriminating inputs (CJK, NFC and NFD accented Latin, Arabic-Indic digits, astral letters U+1D400, Thai, Arabic, Ⅸ/½/ʰ, U+203F undertie, emoji, underscore identifiers, URLs, decimals, "2.7.1.", ".5", "5.", "a.b.c", empty, whitespace-only). Result: 25/25 byte-identical on BOTH the raw token list and the StandardAnalyzer output. Whoosh itself is not installed (ModuleNotFoundError confirmed), so STOP_WORDS could not be validated against the package — I used the contract's locked 34-word list verbatim, which matches the research recall (size 34, includes 'tbd', excludes 'was'/'but'/'they').

Confirmed behaviors: dot-bridging keeps "www.example.com", "1.5", "2.7.1" as single tokens; "end." -> "end"; "a..b" -> "a","b"; "héllo 世界" -> ["héllo","世界"] (bare \w would have given ["llo"]); NFD "éclair" -> ["clair"] (faithful to Python, which splits at the combining mark). Stale-lastIndex regression tested three ways — repeated tokenize() calls on one tokenizer, two interleaved lazy generators from the same tokenizer, and repeated analyze() on one StandardAnalyzer — all correct. Laziness verified: 3 tokens pulled from a 4.6 MB string in 2 ms. No catastrophic backtracking: a single 200 KB token is 3.3 ms, 150 KB of dot-bridged text 1.7 ms, 100 K words 14 ms. renumber=true closes positional gaps (["quick",1],["brown",2],["fox",3]); renumber=false leaves holes (1, 3); removestops=false flags stop words with stopped=true instead of dropping them.

FOR THE FIELDS/WRITER AGENTS: call `analyzer.analyze(value, {positions, chars, mode: 'index'|'query', keeporiginal, removestops, start_pos, start_char})` -> lazy Iterable<Token>; `.call(...)` is an identical alias. TEXT's phrase=true means you should pass positions: true. StandardAnalyzer({stoplist: null}) drops the StopFilter stage entirely (passing an empty list instead would still apply minsize=2 — that distinction is implemented).

I ran an integration simulation of the fieldtypes/writer usage over the exact argv triples in the ground truth. It confirms the consensus: ('','','') , ('x','x','x'), ('1','2','3'), ('-5','2','3'), ('the a of','tbd','A B') all index an EMPTY lexicon (single chars die on minsize=2, stop words on the stop list, '-5' loses the sign and then '5' dies on minsize) while the document count stays 3 — which is exactly why Every() + len(results) must print 3 regardless of input. ('-5.5','2','3') does produce the term "5.5". Nothing in the semantics consensus looks wrong to me.

CROSS-MODULE HAZARD I noticed while reading the source (not my file): line 14 is `Schema(title=TEXT(stored=True), content=TEXT)` — `content` receives the TEXT factory ITSELF, uncalled. Schema must detect a function-valued field and invoke it (Python instantiates the class); otherwise `content` will not be a FieldType and add_document will misbehave.
